procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 24.04.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in CRMBA No. 11828 of 2023, and an order dated 31.10.2023 from a coordinate bench of the High Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 2 (Vivek Pal @ Vikki Pal) filed a bail application under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (“CrPC”) before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad. The High Court allowed the bail application on 24.04.2023 and enlarged Respondent No. 2 on bail subject to certain conditions. A co-accused, Punit Pal, was also enlarged on bail by a coordinate bench of the High Court via an order dated 31.10.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant (Original Complainant) filed appeals in the Supreme Court assailing the correctness of the High Court's orders that enlarged Respondent No. 2 and Punit Pal on bail. The Supreme Court tagged Criminal Appeal No. 2168 of 2024 (filed against the order related to Punit Pal) with Criminal Appeal No. 2169 of 2024 (arising out of SLP(Crl.) No 14988 of 2023). The Supreme Court heard the appeals together and disposed of them with a common judgment because the facts and questions involved were similar.

directions: The bail bond(s) of accused Vivek Pal @ Vikki Pal and Punit Pal shall stand cancelled.
The aforenoted person(s) shall be taken into custody forthwith.
A copy of this judgment shall be forwarded to the Trial Court and PS Lalganj, Basti, Uttar Pradesh for onward action and necessary compliance.
The Trial Court is directed to conclude the trial expeditiously preferably within a period of one year from the date of receipt of copy of this judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court appropriately exercised its discretion under Section 439 of the CrPC while granting bail to the accused persons.

facts: The accused persons were charged with serious offences, including murder (Section 302 IPC), robbery (Section 394 IPC), and criminal conspiracy (Section 120-B IPC).
The trial court had initially rejected their bail applications with well-reasoned orders.
Subsequently, the High Court overturned the trial court's decision and granted bail to the accused.
A weapon used in the assault was recovered from one of the accused.
Charges had already been framed against the accused persons, and they were noted to have overwhelming influence in their area.
law: The grant of bail under Section 439 of the CrPC is a discretionary power.
This discretion must not be exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or injudiciously.
A court must balance the liberty of the individual with the public interest in the administration of justice.

Key factors to be considered include: (i) the seriousness and gravity of the crime, (ii) the conduct of the accused, (iii) the overall impact of the crime on society, and (iv) a prima facie view that the accused committed the offence.
An order granting bail that does not consider these relevant factors suffers from non-application of mind and is liable to be set aside.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had failed to properly apply the established legal principles for granting bail.

It held that the High Court should not have granted bail, giving significant weight to three main factors: the seriousness of the crime (which included murder), the conduct of the accused, and the overall impact of the crime on society, especially given the accused persons' local influence.

The Court also noted that the High Court overlooked other critical aspects, such as the fact that charges had already been framed, a weapon had been recovered from an accused, and the trial court had previously passed a well-reasoned order denying bail.
By ignoring these crucial considerations, the High Court's decision was deemed to be a mechanical exercise of power suffering from a "vice of non-application of mind."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court did not appropriately exercise its discretion under Section 439 of the CrPC. It found the decision to grant bail was made without due application of mind to the gravity of the offence, the conduct of the accused, and other relevant factors. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order granting bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court appropriately exercised its discretion under Section 439 of the CrPC while granting bail to the accused persons.
appellant_arguments: That Respondent No. 2; and Punit Pal have misused their liberty i.e., an identified witness had previously sought police protection.
respondent_arguments: That the allegation levelled against Respondent No. 2; and Punit Pal vis-à-vis extension of threats to the Appellant was wholly erroneous and is in fact, a part of a calculated effort to paint Respondent No. 2; and Punit Pal in bad light.

cases.case_name: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee
cases.principle: For enunciating the parameters on which the correctness of an order granting bail must be evaluated.

cases.case_name: Neeru Yadav v. State of U.P.
cases.principle: For the principle that the discretionary power to grant bail ought not to be used arbitrarily, capriciously, or injudiciously and must consider factors like the seriousness of the crime and the conduct of the accused.
For the principles governing the grant of bail, emphasizing that relevant factors such as the seriousness of the crime, conduct of the accused, and impact on society must be considered.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court's discretionary power to grant bail must be exercised with due application of mind by balancing public interest and individual liberty. An order granting bail is illegal and liable to be set aside if the court fails to consider relevant factors, including: (i) whether there is a prima facie or reasonable ground to believe the accused committed the offence; (ii) the nature and gravity of the accusation; and (iii) the likelihood of the accused obstructing the trial or evading justice.
obiter: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily interfere with a High Court's order granting bail.
At the bail stage, it is not relevant for the court to examine evidence in detail to come to a conclusive finding.
Any observations made in this judgment shall not be treated as an expression of opinion on the merits of the case at trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court ought not to have granted the accused persons bail because it failed to properly apply its mind to the relevant considerations for such a decision. The grant of bail was inappropriate on account of the seriousness of the crime, the conduct of the accused persons, and the overall impact of the crime on society at large, given that the accused persons had overwhelming influence in the area.
legal_tests_applied: The discretion to grant bail under Section 439 of the CrPC ought not to be used arbitrarily, capriciously, and injudiciously.

A court is required to factor, amongst other things, a prima facie view that the accused had committed the offence, the nature and gravity of the offence and the likelihood of the accused obstructing the proceedings of the trial in any manner or evading the course of justice.

When considering a bail application, the court must advert to relevant considerations, including: (i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the offence; (ii) nature and gravity of the accusation; (iii) severity of the punishment in the event of conviction; (iv) danger of the accused absconding or fleeing, if released on bail; (vi) likelihood of the offence being repeated; (vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being influenced; and (viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.
If the High Court does not advert to these relevant considerations and mechanically grants bail, the said order would suffer from the vice of non-application of mind, rendering it to be illegal.
why_appellant_won: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument that the accused had misused their liberty, which factored into the court's consideration of the 'conduct of accused person(s)' as a reason to deny bail.

The High Court's order granting bail was found to suffer from the vice of non-application of mind, as it failed to consider the seriousness of the crime, the conduct of the accused, and their societal influence.
why_respondent_lost: The High Court's exercise of discretion in granting bail was found to be flawed because it did not properly consider the seriousness of the crime, the conduct of the accused, and their overwhelming influence in the area.
The Supreme Court determined that the High Court mechanically granted bail without adverting to the relevant considerations, rendering the order illegal.
policy_considerations: The provision for being released on bail draws an appropriate balance between public interest in the administration of justice and the protection of individual liberty pending adjudication of the case.

The grant of bail is to be secured within the bounds of the law and in compliance with the conditions laid down by this Court. It is for this reason that a court must balance numerous factors that guide the exercise of the discretionary power to grant bail on a case-by-case basis.
